### List

```go
func (s *UserService) List(
	ctx context.Context,
	hostname string,
) (*Response[Collection[UserAccount]], error)
```

List the users of the host.

Lists each user with its IDs, home, shell, groups and whether it is locked,
through gohai: from /etc/passwd, /etc/group and /etc/shadow on Linux, and from
the directory service with dscl on macOS. The groups are those that list the
user as a member, besides its primary group.

It sends `GET /api/node/{hostname}/user`, and needs the permission `user:read`.

The examples of the method's definition:

A host with users, `go run user.go list`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.List(ctx, target)
```

### Create

```go
func (s *UserService) Create(
	ctx context.Context,
	hostname string,
	input UserCreateInput,
) (*Response[Collection[UserResult]], error)
```

Add a user.

Adds the user with useradd, with its home directory, and sets its password with
chpasswd when one is given. The controller hashes the password, so the job and
NATS have only the hash. A user that the host has already does not change and
reports changed: false. It runs on the Debian family only, and elsewhere reports
skipped.

It sends `POST /api/node/{hostname}/user`, and needs the permission
`user:write`.

The examples of the method's definition:

Add a user, `go run user.go create`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Create(ctx, target, client.UserCreateInput{Name: "osapitest"})
```

Add a user with a shell, groups and a password, `go run user.go create-2`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Create(ctx, target, client.UserCreateInput{
	Groups:   []string{"root"},
	Name:     "osapitest",
	Password: "-",
	Shell:    "/bin/sh",
})
```

Add a system user with its IDs and its home, `go run user.go create-3`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Create(ctx, target, client.UserCreateInput{
	GID:    100,
	Home:   "/home/osapitest",
	Name:   "osapitest",
	System: true,
	UID:    1999,
})
```

Get one user.

Reads one user from the same list. A user that the host does not have is not
found.

It sends `GET /api/node/{hostname}/user/{name}`, and needs the permission
`user:read`.

The examples of the method's definition:

A user, `go run user.go get`:

```go

```

### Update

```go
func (s *UserService) Update(
	ctx context.Context,
	hostname string,
	input UserUpdateInput,
) (*Response[Collection[UserResult]], error)
```

Change a user.

Changes what the input gives and the user does not have already, with usermod:
its shell, its home, which usermod moves the files to, its groups, which replace
the groups it has, and whether it is locked. The same values report changed:
false. A user that the host does not have is not found. It runs on the Debian
family only, and elsewhere reports skipped.

It sends `PUT /api/node/{hostname}/user/{name}`, and needs the permission
`user:write`.

The examples of the method's definition:

Set the shell, `go run user.go update`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Update(ctx, target, client.UserUpdateInput{
	Name:  "osapitest",
	Shell: "/bin/bash",
})
```

Move the home, set the groups and lock it, `go run user.go update-2`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Update(ctx, target, client.UserUpdateInput{
	Groups: []string{"root"},
	Home:   "/home/osapitest2",
	Lock:   types.Lock("locked"),
	Name:   "osapitest",
})
```

Unlock it, `go run user.go update-3`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Update(ctx, target, client.UserUpdateInput{
	Lock: types.Lock("unlocked"),
	Name: "osapitest",
})
```

### Delete

```go
func (s *UserService) Delete(
	ctx context.Context,
	hostname string,
	name string,
) (*Response[Collection[UserResult]], error)
```

Remove a user.

Removes the user and its home directory with userdel -r. A user that the host
does not have does not change and reports changed: false. It runs on the Debian
family only, and elsewhere reports skipped.

It sends `DELETE /api/node/{hostname}/user/{name}`, and needs the permission
`user:write`.

The examples of the method's definition:

Remove a user, `go run user.go delete`:

```go
resp, err := c.User.Delete(ctx, target, "osapitest")
```

### RowStatus

What happened on the host: ok, the operation ran and succeeded; failed, it ran
and did not succeed; skipped, the host's OS family does not support it; timeout,
the host did not answer, so nobody knows whether it ran.

A `string`, one of `ok`, `failed`, `skipped`, `timeout`.
